result:
There is an unclaimed territory that exists between destinations. Not quite here, not quite there—the airport gate at 4:17 a.m., the parking garage stairwell humming with fluorescent light, the thirty seconds after a thunderstorm when the air still smells of ozone but the sky has already cleared. We usually rush through these intervals, treating them as dead space, logistical inconvenience, the hollow calories of experience. But if you stop—really stop—you will find they possess a strange clarity that destination moments often lack.

In these interstices, the noise of purpose falls away entirely. At a bus station in winter, you can suddenly hear your own breath. The usual architecture of identity—job title, social obligation, the narrative we are constantly maintaining—loosens its grip. You become, briefly, just a body in space, observing the particular gray of a cloud bank or the way coffee steam dissolves against cold glass. There is no performance required because nobody is watching for an outcome. The world, for a moment, stops asking you to become anything other than present.

I think we fear these pauses more than we admit. Modern life is meticulously engineered to eliminate them—seamless apps, optimized schedules, the constant drip of notification that ensures we are never truly between things. We have become allergic to the unstructured minute. Yet it is precisely in these gaps that we do our quietest thinking, the kind that does not announce itself with urgency but settles like sediment, slowly clarifying what we actually value beneath the noise.

The Japanese have a concept—*ma*—not emptiness, but negative space that gives meaning to form. Every painting needs its blank paper; every symphony needs its rest. Our lives, I believe, need these liminal chambers too. Not as failures of productivity, but as necessary architecture.

So the next time you find yourself in transit, in the rain-slicked pause before entering a building, in the silence between two conversations—do not reach for your phone. Stay a moment longer. There is a kind of truth available only to those who are willing to be lost in between.
